subject: Mathematics
owned_sme_text: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects called elements. The word well-defined is important: there must be a clear rule for deciding whether any given object belongs to the set, with no ambiguity. The collection of tall boys in a class is not a well-defined set because tall is subjective; the collection of boys taller than 170 cm is. Sets are denoted by capital letters and elements by lowercase. Membership is written as a in A; non-membership as a not in A. Sets can be specified by roster method (listing all elements, like A = {2, 4, 6, 8}) or by set-builder notation (giving a rule, like A = {x : x is an even positive integer less than 10}). The empty set, denoted by the symbol phi or {}, contains no elements; the universal set U is the set containing all objects under discussion for a particular context. A set A is a subset of B (written A subset B) if every element of A is also in B. The empty set is a subset of every set. The set of all subsets of a set A is called the power set P(A); if A has n elements, P(A) has 2^n elements. Set operations include union (A union B = {x : x in A or x in B}), intersection (A intersect B = {x : x in A and x in B}), difference (A - B = {x : x in A and x not in B}), and complement (A' = U - A). De Morgan's laws are central: (A union B)' = A' intersect B', and (A intersect B)' = A' union B'. Two sets are equal if and only if they have exactly the same elements; order and repetition do not matter, so {1, 2, 2, 3} = {1, 2, 3} = {3, 1, 2}. Sets are called disjoint if their intersection is empty. The number of elements in a finite set A is denoted n(A) or |A|. For two finite sets, the inclusion-exclusion principle states n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B). For three sets, n(A union B union C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A intersect B) - n(B intersect C) - n(A intersect C) + n(A intersect B intersect C). Venn diagrams give an intuitive visual representation: each set is a region of the plane, and the universal set is the rectangle containing all regions. Common JEE pitfall: confusing the empty set {} with the set containing the empty set {{}} — these are different; the first has zero elements, the second has one element which happens to itself be a set. Another classic trap: applying De Morgan's laws incorrectly by forgetting to flip the operator from union to intersection (or vice versa). For inclusion-exclusion problems with three or more sets, students often miss the higher-order intersection terms, leading to undercounted or overcounted results. JEE Mains problems on sets are usually straightforward — direct application of operations or counting via Venn diagrams; JEE Advanced sometimes embeds sets into a more abstract algebra or function-theory problem.
